questions.q: Which gcc option adds the extra debugging information that GDB uses to find variables and functions and map machine code back to C source lines?
questions.explain: -g adds debugging information to the executable, e.g. gcc -g myprog.c.

questions.q: When building a program for debugging, it is a good idea to also turn on optimizations like -O2, because optimized code maps more clearly back to the C source.
questions.explain: Avoid optimizations when debugging. Optimized machine code often does not map clearly back to the C source, which makes it very hard to debug.

questions.q: Which variant of the debugging flag can sometimes give better results than -g by including extra debugging information?
questions.explain: Some users get better results with -g3, which can include extra debugging information.

questions.q: Right after you run `gdb a.out` and see the (gdb) prompt, the program has not started running yet, so you can set breakpoints before it starts.
questions.explain: GDB shows its prompt before running the program. The program only starts when you type `run`.

questions.q: A program crashed and the operating system dumped a core file. How can GDB help?
choices: GDB can open the core file together with the executable that produced it, and `where` shows the point of the crash
GDB can only use a core file if the program is still running
A core file holds only the program's source code, so GDB uses it in place of -g
Core files are only for Valgrind, not GDB
questions.explain: A core file records the program's state when it crashed. Load it in GDB along with the executable (e.g. gdb core a.out), then use `where` to see where it crashed.

questions.q: What is DDD?
choices: A memory-error checker that replaces GDB
A GUI wrapper around a command-line debugger such as GDB that accepts the same commands
A gcc flag that turns on debug output
A GDB command that dumps the call stack
questions.explain: The Data Display Debugger is a GUI front end for a command-line debugger like GDB. It accepts the same parameters and commands, and it adds menus.

questions.q: When a running program reaches a breakpoint on a given line, what does GDB do?
choices: Pauses before running that line and prints the breakpoint number and source line
Ends the program and prints the call stack
Skips that line and keeps running
questions.explain: GDB pauses before the breakpoint line runs, prints the breakpoint number and source line, and waits for commands.

questions.q: In GDB, what exact command starts a.out from the beginning with the command line arguments 100 and 200?
questions.explain: Put the arguments after `run`, e.g. `run 100 200`.

questions.q: You are paused at `if ( findAndReturnMax(arr, 5, max) != 0 ) {` and want to watch findAndReturnMax run line by line. Which command should you type?
questions.explain: `step` enters the function call and pauses before its first line. `next` would run the whole call as one step.

questions.q: If the next line of C code contains a function call, `next` runs that whole call and its return as one step.
questions.explain: `next` runs the full next line, including any function calls in it. Use `step` to go into the function.

questions.q: Which command lets a paused program keep running until it hits the next breakpoint?
questions.explain: `cont` continues from the current pause point until the next breakpoint. `run` restarts the program from the beginning.

questions.q: Which of these are valid ways to set a breakpoint?
questions.explain: `break` takes a function name (break main, break findAndReturnMax) or a source line number (break 27). `cont` only continues execution.

questions.q: After a `next`, the source line GDB prints has already been executed.
questions.explain: The printed line is where the program is paused, so it is the line that will run next. It has not run yet.

questions.q: What does `display i` do that `print i` does not?
choices: It prints i automatically every time the program pauses at a breakpoint
It sets a breakpoint wherever i changes
questions.explain: `display` makes GDB print the expression automatically each time a breakpoint is hit, e.g. in every loop iteration. `print` shows it only once.

questions.q: You typed `list` and GDB showed lines 29-38. What happens if you type `list` again?
choices: It shows the next lines of source after those
It shows an error, because list only works once per pause
questions.explain: Each later `list` shows the next lines of source. You can also give it a line number (list 11) or a function name (list findAndReturnMax).

questions.q: After `step` enters findAndReturnMax, you can print that function's parameters and local variables (for example `print array1[0]` or `print max`).
questions.explain: Once paused inside the function, its parameters and locals are in scope, and `print` can show them or expressions that use them.

questions.q: In main, `int arr[5] = { 17, 21, 44, 2, 60 };` has run. What does `print arr[3]` show?
questions.explain: `print` evaluates C expressions. arr[3] is the fourth element, 2. (`print arr` would show the whole array.)

questions.q: Which GDB commands print the call stack?
questions.explain: `where` and `bt` (backtrace) both print the call stack. `frame` switches to a given stack frame, and `list` shows source code.

questions.q:
`where` prints:
#0  findAndReturnMax (array1=0x7fffffffe290, len=5, max=17) at badprog.c:21
#1  0x0000555555554810 in main (argc=1, argv=0x7fffffffe398) at badprog.c:40
Which statement is correct?
choices: main is at the top of the stack and paused at line 21
findAndReturnMax is at the top of the stack (frame 0), and main (frame 1) is at line 40, where it calls findAndReturnMax
findAndReturnMax has already returned to main
Frame 1 is the function currently running
questions.explain: Frame 0 is the top of the stack, the function currently running. main is below it in frame 1, at line 40, where it calls findAndReturnMax.

questions.q: You are paused inside findAndReturnMax and want to check the values main passed to it. What should you do?
choices: Type `frame 1` to switch to main's frame, then `print arr` and `print max`
Type `run` again with a breakpoint at main
Nothing; main's local variables can't be inspected while another function is running
questions.explain: `frame N` switches to that stack frame, so you can inspect the caller's locals and parameters without resuming the program.

questions.q: `frame 1` resumes the program until control returns to the caller in frame 1.
questions.explain: `frame` does not run any code. It only switches the context GDB uses, so you can inspect that frame's variables.

questions.q: badprog.c's findAndReturnMax loops with `for (i=1; i <= len; i++)` and reads array1[i]. It is called with a 5-element array and len = 5. What is the largest index i it reads?
questions.explain: The loop runs while i <= 5, so the last iteration reads array1[5]. The valid indexes are only 0-4.

questions.q: With `display array1[i]` turned on, the last breakpoint hit shows i = 5 and array1[i] = 32767, but 32767 is not in the array. What does this show?
choices: The array was initialized wrong in main
The loop reads past the end of the array; 32767 is just whatever is in memory there
GDB cannot show array elements reliably
questions.explain: Index 5 is outside a 5-element array, so the loop reads past its end. The loop condition should be i < len.

questions.q: Which loop header fixes the out-of-bounds bug in findAndReturnMax (array length len, starting from i = 1 because max starts as array1[0])?
questions.explain: The loop must stop before index len, so the condition should be i < len.

questions.q: findAndReturnMax(int *array1, int len, int max) sets max to 60 (a breakpoint at line 30 shows this). Yet after it returns, `print max` in main shows 17. Why?
choices: max was passed by value, so the function changed only its own copy, and the function returns 0, not max
The breakpoint at line 30 reset max
main's arr holds different values than array1
questions.explain: The max parameter is a copy of main's max. Changing it inside the function does not change main's variable, and the function returns 0 instead of max.

questions.q: Which changes would let main get the maximum that findAndReturnMax computes?
choices: Have findAndReturnMax return its max value, and use that return value in main
Add a pass-by-pointer parameter that the function uses to update main's max
Change the parameter name from max to result
Set a breakpoint on the return statement
questions.explain: The function needs to send the value back, either as its return value or through a pointer to main's max. Renaming the parameter or adding breakpoints changes nothing.

questions.q: When a program crashes while running under GDB, GDB pauses it at the point of the crash so you can examine its state.
questions.explain: GDB takes control at the crash, e.g. 'Program received signal SIGSEGV', and you can then use where, list, print, frame, and so on.

questions.q: Name the signal GDB reports when a program crashes with a segmentation fault.
questions.explain: GDB prints 'Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.'

questions.q: segfaulter crashes at `array[i] = i;` in initfunc. `print i` shows 1, `print array[i]` says 'Cannot access memory at address 0x4', and `print array` shows (int *) 0x0. What caused the crash?
choices: array is a NULL pointer, and array[i] dereferences it
The program was not compiled with -g
questions.explain: The array's base address is 0 (NULL). Dereferencing a null pointer through array[i] crashes the program.

questions.q: After `frame 1` in segfaulter, main's code shows `int *arr = NULL;` followed by `initfunc(arr, 100)`, and `print arr` shows 0x0. What is the fix?
choices: Change the loop in initfunc to start at i = 0
Allocate memory for arr with malloc() before calling initfunc
questions.explain: main passes a NULL pointer because arr was never allocated. Allocating space for arr with malloc() fixes the crash.

questions.q: Right after a crash in GDB, which commands are most useful for finding where it happened?
questions.explain: `where` shows the call stack, with the function and line of the crash. `list` shows the source code around that point.
